items.lbText:
Lawsuit also alleging pressure on hardware suppliers comes after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching employees

OpenAI sued Apple on Friday, accusing the company of ⁠stealing its trade secrets ​and discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.

The suit, filed in northern California federal court, comes after Apple sued OpenAI for allegedly poaching its employees to gain access to its technology.

OpenAI filed the counterclaims ⁠in California federal court on Friday, saying that Apple’s employment practices were designed to “trap” employees and prevent them from working on competitors’ technology.

OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal electronic devices that threaten to “outcompete Apple on what ⁠Apple views as its own turf”, the company said in its Friday court filing.

OpenAI said in the filing that Apple ​gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who worked ‌at OpenAI for six months. In ‌that time, the employee gained access to specific information on a new device as well as OpenAI’s roadmap for future hardware ‌products.

“Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place,” OpenAI said.

Apple denied using the rehired employee to access OpenAI’s confidential information and denied trying to suppress competition in AI device manufacturing.

“OpenAI’s counterclaims are a transparent attempt to distract from the substance of Apple’s lawsuit,” Apple said in a Friday statement.

Tensions between the two tech companies have escalated as the intensifying race to develop AI products fuels competition for ‌talent and proprietary technology.

Apple sued OpenAI and the former Apple employees Tang Tan and Chang Liu in July, alleging misappropriation of its trade secrets to benefit the ChatGPT owner’s foray into consumer hardware.

Tan, ​a 24-year Apple employee who was a vice-president of product design for iPhone and Apple Watch, was part of the group that launched the AI device startup io Products before it was acquired by OpenAI in 2025.

OpenAI and the employees have denied those allegations and said that Apple’s lawsuit depended on its unauthorized monitoring of Liu’s personal messages after he stopped working for Apple. OpenAI and ⁠attorneys for Tan and Liu did not immediately respond to a request for comment on ​Friday’s court filing.

In Friday’s filing, OpenAI criticized ​Apple for encouraging employees to do work on ​their personal Apple devices and accounts, then preventing those employees from an orderly separation of work and ​personal accounts when they leave ‌for new jobs.

OpenAI said ​that Apple continues to access ​former employees’ personal devices and accounts after they leave the company, enabling Apple to “monitor and ensnare departing employees” when they leave for competitors.

OpenAI said that 400 employees have left Apple for OpenAI so far, and Apple wants to intimidate other employees from leaving to find other tech companies.

items.title: Thousands still without power after storms that snarled Thanksgiving travel
items.author: Edward Helmore and agencies
items.content:
Heavy rains and high winds downed trees and power lines and led to water rescues from New York to Virginia

Skies cleared along the US eastern seaboard on Friday, and power was being restored to hundreds of thousands of customers whose Thanksgiving plans were disrupted by heavy rains and high winds that swept over the region a day earlier.

The storms snarled travel, downed trees and power lines and led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. At its peak, nearly a million customers were without power.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Homes without power, travel disrupted and Macy’s Thanksgiving parade postponed for first time in New York

Storms have flooded communities on the US east coast, knocking out power to nearly a million customers and prompting the first-ever postponement of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City.

High winds and flooding hammered both coasts, disrupting holiday travel. More than 900,000 homes and businesses were without electricity on Thursday evening, with the majority in east coast states, according to the outage tracking website PowerOutage.us. More than 2,200 flights to or from US destinations were delayed and more than 400 were cancelled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.

Macy’s postponed the annual Thanksgiving parade until Saturday because of concerns about how the parade’s large balloons would fare in the windswept canyons between Manhattan’s skyscrapers.

Torrential rain, high winds and flooding pounded sections of the east coast. New Jersey was under a state of emergency, along with parts of New York. The weather service posted wind advisories from northern Georgia to most of the mid-Atlantic and southern New England.

People were rescued from their cars in New York City because of flooding, said the mayor, Zohran Mamdani, and similar rescues were reported in other coastal communities.

“There is no destination worth your safety,” Mamdani said.

Strong winds and flooding disrupted train lines, toppled trees and caused power outages on Thanksgiving night, New York City emergency management officials said. Several scaffolding structures collapsed in the wind, but no injuries were reported.

The storms also flooded areas from North Carolina through to New Jersey as high tide rolled in. Roads were closed, and emergency workers were rescuing people from cars stranded in water.

Avalon, New Jersey, was seeing some of the worst flooding in its history, said Scott J Wahl, the borough’s business administrator.

“Not quite Hurricane Sandy,” Wahl said, referring to the benchmark storm for his village on the far south end of New Jersey’s Atlantic coast.

Flood waters washed debris over the road, and a few drivers were rescued after driving around barricades into the waters, but no injuries were reported, Wahl said.

Lance Miller, 54, said flood waters in his Ocean City, New Jersey, neighbourhood were about a foot deep and that driving to the nearest supermarket would probably “destroy your car”.

Miller said he would be staying indoors and having Thanksgiving dinner with his wife and daughter. But he said some of his friends were “not so lucky” and had flooding inside their homes.

The Margate City fire department near Atlantic City, New Jersey posted video on Facebook of water pouring through the city’s streets, even before heavy rains started.

A firefighter said the tide was coming in ferociously, even with an hour to go before its peak. Water closed in on houses, and sandbags were piled in front of businesses.

Some highways and bridges were temporarily closed. The nearly 18-mile (29-km) Chesapeake Bay bridge-tunnel in southern Virginia was closed for several hours on Thursday morning because of high winds, while NC 12, the only highway connecting Hatteras Island on the North Carolina Outer Banks to the mainland, was closed after seawater breached the dunes and covered the two-lane highway.

In Maryland, nearly 2 million water customers in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to conserve water because of intermittent power disruptions associated with the storm. Baltimore police closed several streets on Thursday night after storm surge caused flooding in waterfront neighborhoods.

The storms also prompted several brief tornado warnings on Thursday, including a rare twister south-east of Seattle, Washington.

The US president, Donald Trump, signed a disaster declaration on Thursday for Florida in response to earlier flooding that damaged hundreds of homes and required water rescues. Trump had approved funding earlier this week, but gathered local officials on Thanksgiving to talk about it in a small signing ceremony at his home in West Palm Beach.

Trump was asked about aid for Thursday’s storms on the east coast. “Well, we’re going to look at that. We have some requests from others,” he said.

Heavy snow fell on parts of Illinois and Missouri with St Louis recording 7.3in (18.5cm) of snowfall. Sainte Genevieve, Missouri, recorded 14in.

The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, which hosts hockey and other ice skating activities, was empty when the roof caved in at about 3 am, according to the city.

Meanwhile, high-tide driven waves and strong winds caused flooding along the Pacific coast on Thursday. The conditions were expected into Friday, according to the National Weather Service.

Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations in areas from Humboldt county in the far north to Ventura county near Los Angeles.

King tides were surging along the west coast.

Video showed a big wave tearing down part of the Pacifica pier in California on Wednesday, sending it into the ocean. Officials had closed the L-shaped pier in the summer after finding cracks.

Amtrak’s Pacific Surfliner posted more than a dozen itinerary changes on social media on Thursday morning, starting with one that said trains could not run through San Clemente “due to track damage”. It also suspended service between Irvine and Oceanside because of washouts caused by high tide conditions. Service was further shut down from San Diego north to Oceanside and up to Los Angeles international airport.

items.lbText:
Hundreds of thousands of Canadians call for Pete Hoekstra to be declared ‘persona non grata’

A petition signed by nearly 290,000 Canadians calling on Mark Carney’s government to oust Pete Hoekstra as US ambassador to Canada was formally presented to the House of Commons on Thursday, a sign of the strained relations between the neighboring countries.

Elizabeth May, a Canadian Green party member, originally opened the petition for signatures in July 2026 after a woman from Calgary sponsored it. The petition requests that the Canadian government declare Hoekstra “persona non grata” due to his “US” diplomatic interference in Canadian domestic affairs”.

“He has been repeatedly abusive and insulting to Canadians,” May said as she formally introduced the petition, according to Politico .

She called Donald Trump’s envoy “the most undiplomatic diplomat” Canada had ever seen.

The petition accuses Hoekstra of “undermining” Canada-US diplomatic relations through repeated statements about Canadian politics that its signatories say are “inconsistent with diplomatic protocol”.

The US state department did not immediately return a request for comment.

Hoekstra is a deeply polarizing figure in Canada, particularly for his response to Trump’s desire to annex the country and make Canada the 51st US state.

Speaking to a Michigan radio station last year, he described the president’s rhetoric as a “sign of affection” and questioned why Canadians were offended by what he characterized as a “generous offer”.

Hoekstra also previously described Canada’s 2025 federal election that saw a remarkable come-from-behind victory for the prime minister’s Liberal party as “anti-American”.

The US ambassador had suggested Canada could be blamed if Republicans performed poorly in this month’s midterm elections.

“That’s an interesting way of framing it,” Carney replied, when asked about the comments.

Democrats swept the November elections, including key Senate races in border states such as Michigan and Maine, where the bitter tariff war between Washington and Ottawa has hit residents hard.

Last month Carney said American tariffs hurt both American and Canadian households. He added that auto exports to the US had so far fallen 10%, and US exports to Canada have fallen by more than 20%.

“US tariffs have upended a trade bargain that’s existed for decades,” Carney said. “They’ve raised costs for American families while putting Ontario workers and businesses at a disadvantage and under a cloud of uncertainty.”

Hoekstra had also accused Canada of potential “political interference” in the US election, a claim Carney said held “no merit”. Speaking to reporters in Turkey, the prime minister said he was “disappointed that their envoy sees that as his role, to make these suggestions”.

Even though the Canadian government is required to provide a formal response to the petition presented by May, the petition is nonbinding.

“I think the government will quite likely say, ‘No, we’re not prepared to declare Pete Hoekstra persona non grata and strip him of his diplomatic credentials,’”, May said in an interview with CTV .

Despite this possibility, May expects the petition to signal to Trump that the Canadian government has the support of its constituents, and she hopes the government can use it as leverage against Trump with Democrats holding power in Congress for the second half of Trump’s term.

items.author: Caroline Davies
items.content:
Police are working with agencies across Europe after similar incidents occurred at two other Don Toliver concerts

Greater Manchester police said they were working to identify the suspects and the substance involved during the incident at the Co-op Live Arena on Sunday evening.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Police are working with agencies across Europe after similar incidents occurred at two other Don Toliver concerts

A group of organised criminals are believed to have carried out robberies during Don Toliver’s Manchester concert, where an “unknown substance” was released , police have said, with similar incidents having occurred at another two of the US rapper’s gigs in Europe.

Greater Manchester police said they were working to identify the suspects and the substance involved during the incident at the Co-op Live Arena on Sunday evening.

No arrests have been made but mobile phone and CCTV footage is being reviewed by officers, a police statement said. The force is working with other law enforcement agencies across Europe after similar incidents at two Toliver gigs, which officers believe are “relevant” to their inquiries.

Eighty-nine people displayed symptoms believed to be linked to exposure to the substance during the performance in Manchester . The venue was evacuated and a major incident declared as those in the crowd described a “horrible smell”, which police initially believed to be teargas.

Footage shared on social media appeared to show concertgoers coughing and covering their mouths as they left the venue, and medical officials urged anyone who had become unwell after leaving to get in touch. Some of the dozens assessed by doctors reported eye and respiratory symptoms.

Tom Harding, Greater Manchester police assistant chief constable, said: “We’re working to identify those suspects and the substance that we believe was released in the crowd as part of these incidents. All of this work is ongoing at pace.

“There are similar incidents at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe that are also relevant to our inquiries. We’re in contact with law enforcement involved in those investigations.

“No arrests have been made, but our detectives are working through footage captured on mobile phones and CCTV. There are over a 100 people at the gig we are working to try to contact to assist with our inquiries. We thank all those that have assisted us so far.”

Harding said the force was aware some people had been affected psychologically during the Co-op Live incident because of the 2017 terror attack at the Manchester Arena where 22 people were killed by the suicide-bomber Salman Abedi.

He added: “We also know many more people were impacted on the night and afterwards, physically and psychologically. What happened on Sunday night and the imagery on our TVs and online will bring back painful memories of 2017.

“Thankfully, we are not dealing with an incident of such a devastating nature or motive; however, we understand the impact this is likely to have caused.”

items.lbText:
Closely watched decision exposes tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights

Canada’s top court has largely upheld a controversial secularism law in the province of Quebec barring public sector workers from wearing conspicuous religious symbols, in a closely watched decision that exposes the tensions between minority rights and the power of government to override those rights.

In a 6-1 ruling released on Friday morning , the supreme court found Quebec was permitted to shield the law, Bill 21, from most court challenges on the grounds that it violated charter rights.

“Bill 21 is rooted in Quebec’s legitimate and historical commitment to ensuring the laicity of the state in a free and democratic society,” chief justice Richard Wagner wrote in the majority opinion.

Canada’s top court says the four days of hearings from earlier in the year marked one of the longest in its 151-year history. Fifty-one interveners participated, including six attorneys general – also a record number. The court’s website crashed on Friday morning when the judgment was released.

While the judgment was celebrated by some in Quebec who considered it a vindication of the province’s fight, it was swiftly criticised by religious civil liberties groups.

“We cannot exist in a country as free people, where governments can literally go to the electorate and say, ‘I’m gonna take away the rights of a certain group of minorities’, because it’s popular and to play wedge politics with the charter rights of Canadians,” Stephen Brown, chief executive of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, told reporters at a press conference. “If that is the case, we don’t have a charter of rights and freedoms. We have a charter of suggestions and permissions.”

Passed in 2019, Quebec’s secularism law, Bill 21, bars workers including lawyers, judges, police and teachers from wearing religious symbols such as a hijab, turban, kippah or a cross while on the job.

Central to the case – and the reason provincial governments across the country are closely watching the result – is the “notwithstanding clause”, a constitutional mechanism that allows elected governments to override certain fundamental rights and freedoms guaranteed by Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The clause is the result of political compromise from the 1980s, when the federal government set out to replace the existing British North America Act with a new constitution. Provinces feared that under a new constitution, courts would become too powerful, undermining the authority of the elected government. A compromise was hashed out: in cases when a government – provincial or federal – felt that the courts had overstepped, they could invoke the clause to override certain charter rights of citizens.

Some fundamental rights, including protections of religious freedom, equality and speech, could be suspended. But voting, as well as language rights, were untouchable, ensuring Canadians could remove a government if they wanted. A government could only invoke the clause for five years. Before they could renew it, they would first have to face voters .

In its decision, the supreme court rejected most arguments that Bill 21 violated portions of the charter that are not subject to the notwithstanding clause, including guarantees relating to the equality of men and women and the education rights of Quebec’s English-speaking minority.

Quebec’s use of the clause with Bill 21 was notable – and controversial – in that it was the first time the notwithstanding clause had been invoked pre-emptively in an attempt to shield the law from court challenges. Quebec also passed Bill 96 , which sought to strengthen French language protections – again pre-emptively invoking the notwithstanding clause.

But groups affected by those laws can still challenge them and many teachers, religious and civil liberties groups argued it was a clear violation of constitutional rights and reflected government overreach. Quebec’s government has defended the law, saying it is constitutionally valid.

In April 2021, a Quebec superior court judge described the effects of the law as “cruel”, saying it “dehumanises” the people it targets, but conceded the statute could not be struck down because it was protected by the notwithstanding clause. Quebec’s court of appeal also upheld the law in February 2024 on the same grounds.

In its 520-page judgment, the court did find that element of the law infringed on democratic rights protected by the charter, including preventing elected members of Quebec’s National Assembly who wear face coverings for religious reasons from participating in the legislative process.

In a 4-3 decision, the court also endorsed the ability of lower courts to issue “judicial declarations” on laws protected by the notwithstanding clause, giving judges the power to declare a law in violation of the charter, even though the law would be permitted to stand.

The court’s decision was celebrated in Quebec, where the governing Parti Québécois has looked for wedges with the federal government and institutions like the supreme court.

The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, had previously said his province’s right to decide its own laws was at risk.

Canada only recently fended off a threat to national unity after voters in Alberta rejected the initial stages of a separatist push. But Quebec’s newly elected government has shown an eagerness to clash with the prime minister, Mark Carney.

The supreme court’s judgment comes on the same day an appeal will be heard regarding a superior court decision that forces Quebec’s members of the national assembly to swear allegiance to King Charles to sit in the Salon Bleu – the chamber of the assembly. Lawmakers from a number of parties in the province recently refused to swear the oath of allegiance.

items.title: Jess Wilson’s plan for Melbourne sewage plants risks water and wetlands without bringing debt down, experts say
items.author: Josh Taylor
items.content:
Academic says Victorian Liberal proposal to privatise treatment plants and generate profit with no compromise of services ‘a total furphy’

Experts have warned the Victorian Liberals’ plan to lease Melbourne’s sewage treatment plants is a “smoke and mirrors” way to pay off debt that risks compromising the state’s water resources and crucial wetlands for nearly a century.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Academic says Victorian Liberal proposal to privatise treatment plants and generate profit with no compromise of services ‘a total furphy’

Victorian election 2026 guide: what you need to know

Confused about who to vote for? Check the parties’ key promises and policies

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

Experts have warned the Victorian Liberals’ plan to lease Melbourne’s sewage treatment plants is a “smoke and mirrors” way to pay off debt that risks compromising the state’s water resources and crucial wetlands for nearly a century.

On Thursday – two days out from the election – the opposition leader, Jess Wilson, announced plans for a 90-year lease of the Eastern and Western treatment plants , which process the vast majority of the city’s sewage and are run by Melbourne Water.

The lease is estimated to be worth $9.2bn, with Wilson saying there would be “no change” to water bills or the Essential Services Commission’s regulation of prices across the sector.

Experts are concerned the move could lead to worse services for Victorians, and compromise vital wetlands in Melbourne’s west.

Dr Erin O’Donnell, a water law expert at the University of Melbourne law school, said given the prices would still be regulated, it would be difficult for private companies to extract value from the services, and the money gained from the lease would amount to only about 5% of the debt held by the state.

“I wouldn’t even classify it as a sugar hit – it’s smoke and mirrors,” O’Donnell said.

“This will not make a significant dent in the debt that Victoria holds, and we are compromising the future of our water resources 90 years into the future.”

O’Donnell said Victoria already required corporations to pay significant dividends to the state government, with strict controls over pricing. It means there is no profit to be realised for private owners while also delivering the same quality of services, she said.

“Victoria has some of the lowest water charges of anywhere in Australia and the idea that there is unrealised profit that could be safely stripped out without compromising those services is a total furphy – I can’t say it any clearer.”

O’Donnell and Prof Stuart Khan, a water quality expert and head of the school of civil engineering at the University of Sydney, both pointed to the UK privatisation of water services in the 1980s under Margaret Thatcher as an example of how it can all go wrong.

The privatisation has been described as an “unmitigated disaster” , with hopes the Burnham Labour government will renationalise the utilities following years of declining services, and rivers polluted by private operators .

Khan said the UK’s services were privatised without guardrails around pricing or minimum standards of services.

“Practically every single river in England now has sewage contamination in it,” he said. “That’s the sort of situation that we need to make sure that we avoid because obviously private players are only going to be there if there’s a profit to be made.”

Victoria’s Labor state minister for the environment, Jaclyn Symes, pointed to the UK system and said it resulted in bills going up by 40% and “left wildlife swimming in a toilet”.

Khan said the NSW government’s privatisation of Sydney’s desalination plant could be a model that would work.

“It’s price regulated. It has requirements around managing water quality and they put drinking water straight into Sydney’s distribution system,” he said, adding it also has requirements from NSW Health and the state’s environmental protection agency.

Biodiversity Council member and waterbird and wetland expert Prof Richard Kingsford warned the privatisation could have disastrous consequences for Melbourne’s environment, including the wetland in the Western treatment plant at Werribee.

In 1983, the site was listed under the Ramsar convention as an internationally significant wetland, and more than 300 species of bird – including many threatened species such as the orange bellied-parrot – have been recorded there.

“It’s absolutely one of the more important wetland systems,” Kingsford said.

“I think it’s becoming increasingly important because we’ve had more wetlands drying up, less flooding and, particularly in dry times, it provides dependable habitat.”

Kingsford said privatisation “would likely drive different ways of management that might actually not have any consideration for the environmental value of the system”.

O’Donnell said it was “extraordinarily disingenous” for the Liberal party to announce the policy less than two days before the election when many Victorians had already voted.

“I think there is a real concern there, in terms of the openness around their policies [and] this will have significant implications for things like a swimmable Birrarung [Yarra River],” she said.

A Victorian Liberal party spokesperson said the criticism was “another desperate scare campaign by Labor.”

“We are not selling Melbourne Water . It was Labor that had a plan to privatise Melbourne Water. What we are proposing is a lease. When you lease something you still own it.

“The proceeds will be used to reduce Victoria’s debt and interest bill.”

The proposal has already been thrown into doubt after One Nation’s Victorian leader, Warren Pickering, vowed to block it should the party hold the balance of power after the election.

The Greens leader, Ellen Sandell, also promised to “fight Jess Wilson’s privatisation agenda tooth and nail should her Coalition form government”.

items.title: Labor faces prospect of electoral wipeout in Victoria as voters turn to Liberals and One Nation
items.author: Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent
items.content:
Former ALP strategist says Ben Carroll government at risk of losing more than 30 seats in Saturday’s election, to fall behind Pauline Hanson’s party

The Victorian Labor government is facing an electoral wipeout after 12 years in office as the state heads to the polls on Saturday.

Polling during the campaign has consistently pointed to a Coalition victory. The final Newspoll, released on Thursday, showed the Coalition 15 points ahead on a two-party-preferred basis.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Former ALP strategist says Ben Carroll government at risk of losing more than 30 seats in Saturday’s election, to fall behind Pauline Hanson’s party

Victorian election 2026 guide: what you need to know

Confused about who to vote for? Check the parties’ key promises and policies

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

The Victorian Labor government is facing an electoral wipeout after 12 years in office as the state heads to the polls on Saturday.

Polling during the campaign has consistently pointed to a Coalition victory. The final Newspoll, released on Thursday, showed the Coalition 15 points ahead on a two-party-preferred basis.

If replicated across the state, that swing would translate into 67 seats for the Coalition – comfortably above the 45 needed to form a majority government. The Liberals and Nationals currently hold a combined 29 seats.

But the scale of Labor’s defeat remains unclear. Some polls have suggested the party could fall behind One Nation into third place, with its primary vote only marginally ahead of the Greens.

“Right now, definitely, it’s going to be a Coalition government, but how Labor, the Greens and One Nation are going to go – that’s going to be a lot more chaotic,” said Ben Raue, an electoral analyst and founder of the Tally Room.

Raue said One Nation’s prospects will depend heavily on which party it is competing against in each seat. One Nation is targeting 12 lower house seats. It will field candidates in all lower house seats.

In contests with the Liberals or Nationals, One Nation would fare “very badly” because about 80% of preferences from other parties would flow to the Coalition partners, he said.

“The places where they are likely going to be strongest are those outer suburban seats they could take off Labor,” Raue said.

“They probably couldn’t take them if Labor was in a stronger position. Labor is so weak right now that those areas can come into play.”

On Friday, Labor campaign sources said they were bracing for a “wild night”, with three- and four-cornered contests expected across the state. Internal research suggested the party could lose up to 10 seats to One Nation, prompting former premier Steve Bracks to urge voters not to abandon Labor .

One Nation’s state leader, Warren Pickering, tempered expectations, telling reporters on Friday: “We have effectively got one state member, anything more than that is a success. We have already won.”

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a pollster with Redbridge, said Labor was at risk of losing more than 30 seats – a figure he described as conservative. The party currently holds 54.

“If they come out of this with 20 seats, it’s a really good result,” Samaras said. “Below that, without stating the obvious, it’s a massive problem.”

Samaras said Labor was likely to lose several regional seats, including Ripon, Bendigo East – held by former premier Jacinta Allan – Bendigo West, Eureka and Wendouree. The party could also lose seats across the Geelong region that it has held since 1999, including Bellarine, Geelong, Lara and South Barwon.

In Melbourne’s south-east, Carrum and Frankston were also at risk of switching from Labor to One Nation. Further out, Labor was not in contention in Bass, Hastings and Pakenham, where the contest was shaping as a fight between the Liberals and One Nation, he said.

In the north-west, Melton, Sunbury and Sydenham were also potential One Nation gains. Meanwhile, the Liberals are expected to pick up eastern suburbs seats including Ashwood, Bayswater, Box Hill, Glen Waverley and Ringwood.

The Liberals are even confident in the premier’s own seat of Niddrie and neighbouring Essendon.

Labor’s inner-city seats of Footscray, Northcote and Pascoe Vale were each a “coin toss” between the party and the Greens, Samaras said. But Greens sources are confident about the seats, as well as Prahran, which it lost to the Liberals at a 2025 byelection.

Samaras said the margins in many seats would be fragile.

“The Coalition is going to win 55 to 60 seats but someone only has to breathe in the wrong direction and they lose 20,” he said.

The premier, Ben Carroll , made his final pitch to voters on Friday, saying while Labor had “made some mistakes”, it was the only party on the side of workers in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis.

“We won’t fight against you. We won’t make cuts. We certainly won’t say one thing and then, after several million people have voted, then go and do another,” he said, in reference to the Coalition’s pre-budget costings on Thursday, which detailed a plan to privatise the sewage system.

The Coalition leader, Jess Wilson , called the poll a “a referendum on four more years of Labor”.

“Tomorrow Victorians have an opportunity to change the direction of the state we all love and we have the plan to get started,” she said.

If elected on Saturday, she will become Victoria’s youngest leader since federation and the first woman to be popularly elected as the state’s premier – a feat neither Allan nor Joan Kirner achieved.

Additional reporting by Bertin Huynh and Henry Belot

items.title: Momentous decision looms after judges call for Netanyahu charges to be dropped
items.author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
items.content:
Dropping of corruption charges against Israeli PM after unusual intervention could set damaging precedent

The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Dropping of corruption charges against PM after highly unusual intervention could set damaging precedent

The Israeli judges presiding over Benjamin Netanyahu’s corruption trial have called on prosecutors to end proceedings, a highly unusual intervention that leaves the attorney general facing a momentous political decision.

The prime minister has been charged with bribery, fraud and breach of trust in three complex and overlapping criminal cases that hinge on his relationship with telecoms magnates and other wealthy businessmen. Ending the trial without a ruling could set damaging precedents for media independence and how politicians are held to account.

“There were evidentiary difficulties in the case, but the position the judges laid out effectively means abandoning the media to the whims of politicians and publishers, and setting an impossible bar for conviction in corruption cases,” said Yael Freidson, the legal correspondent for Haaretz, who has covered the trial since it began in 2020.

The judges urged prosecutors to drop one case because “the chances of a conviction are low”, seek a plea deal in a second, and reconsider the third set of charges. Even if prosecutors were to prove the allegations of fraud and breach of trust in that case, it was not clear that Netanyahu’s alleged behaviour amounted to criminal conduct, they said.

The attorney general, Gali Baharav-Miara, who was summoned to court to hear the judges’ statement in person, must now decide whether to accept their recommendations and end a trial that has dominated and shaped Israeli politics for the best part of a decade.

The decision is not straightforward, even though the current bench has in effect indicated a not guilty verdict is a foregone conclusion. If the trial continues, their ruling could still be appealed to a higher court, where fresh judges could take a different stance.

“[The former prime minister] Ehud Olmert was acquitted on all charges by the district court and was subsequently convicted by the supreme court on a minor charge,” Ben Caspit wrote in Maariv. “It ain’t over till it’s over.”

“[Baharav-Miara] could opt to reach a lenient plea bargain agreement with the defendant and put it all to rest, but that would be an admission of the entire justice system’s failure and would further fuel the conspiracy theories that Netanyahu and his disciples have been pumping ever since he was indicted.”

Settling or dropping all charges would immediately and permanently absolve Netanyahu, ending the threat of jail time and dispelling the legal shadow hanging over his political future.

A bill making its way through the opposition-controlled parliament would in effect bar him from serving as prime minister until the trial was concluded.

Netanyahu, who has pleaded not guilty to all charges, claims he is the victim of a political witch-hunt and welcomed the judges’ recommendation as a vindication. “The truth has finally come to light,” he said.

Baharav-Miara has withstood pressure from the judges in the case twice before. In 2023 and in 2025 they urged prosecutors to drop bribery charges, the most serious ones that Netanyahu faces, although they stopped short of suggesting the whole trial should be wrapped up.

Perhaps the single point of agreement between Netanyahu’s supporters and his critics in relation to the trial is concern that it has been allowed to drag on for too long. Testimony from Netanyahu had extended over a year and a half, across 98 hearings, the longest by a single witness in Israeli judicial history, Freidson said. The transcripts from all the hearings run to more than 60,000 pages.

Oren Persico has sat in every hearing since the case began in 2020, covering it for the investigative magazine The Seventh Eye. Over that period he watched the judges slowly lose control of their courtroom, he said.

“It started with giving the defence a lot of rope to do what they wanted. Netanyahu’s lawyer lashed out at the prosecution and humiliated them, almost every day, and attacked the judges, which should be an absolute red line in court,” he said. “I think the judges are afraid and tired; they just want to get it all over with.”

The sense of a bench cracking under pressure was exacerbated by the recommendation to reconsider charges in one of the cases against Netanyahu. These were laid out by prosecutors seven years ago, and have not changed since, prompting joking questions about whether the judges had even read the indictment, and serious ones about their political judgment.

When Netanyahu was indicted, he decided to fight the charges both inside and outside the courtroom, declaring war on the prosecution, the media, the police and key democratic and judicial institutions, Persico said.

“To keep himself out of jail, he tried to form an authoritarian state here in Israel, which tore apart society. I understand the interest in putting an end to that,” Persico said. “But ending the trial would send a terrible message to criminals and politicians and media bosses: that if you fight strongly enough you can get away with anything.”

items.title: Mad about mara: the DIY dance movement helping young Nigerians escape the daily grind
items.author: Eromo Egbejule in Lagos
items.content:
What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape

As a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
What started as one artist’s response to being cut out of a music video has exploded, becoming a driving force in Nigeria’s cultural landscape

A s a student in the central Nigerian city of Ilorin, Lawal Habeeb Kola loved staying in his hostel room to produce beats rather than returning to his family house in Lagos, the more frenetic city of his birth.

In 2022, one of his beats became popular on TikTok, and a version featuring ad-libbed vocals from a hypeman sent it viral. He was invited to the music video shoot in Lagos and thought his big break had finally come, but when the video was released, he was absent.

“I was in a restaurant and everybody was anticipating seeing me, but my face did not show once,” the 27-year old, known as DJ Khalipha, said. “I felt disgraced. I stopped posting the song.”

Khalipha retreated to his dorm and revisited the DIY “cruise beats” genre of dance music that he had previously worked in. Taking its name from the pidgin expression “catch cruise”, meaning to joke around, cruise beats is a lo-fi, frenetic genre that incorporates amusing voice samples from Nollywood and memes.

Khalipha raised the already fast 115-120 beats per minute of cruise beats to 140-150bpm, added melancholic undertones and named the new style mara , meaning to lose one’s senses. The popularity of the sound soared, eventually crossing over from the Lagos underground and becoming incorporated into the sound of mainstream musicians.

As the genre exploded, Khalipha lost creative control. “It became a trend that every producer and DJ was hopping on,” said Feranmi Abiola, 24, who directed the 2025 documentary Mara Mania. “They were making sounds and whether it was mara sound or not, they would just title it mara fever, mara this, mara that.”

Like its predecessors, mara’s spread was driven by choreography. One dancer, Obi “Odogwu Mara” Madubogwu, named himself after the sound and dropped dance routines on social media weekly, gaining street credibility. His death in unclear circumstances at the age of 26 galvanised interest in mara, especially among young Nigerians for whom posting and responding to dance challenges in his style became a form of escape from poor job prospects in Nigeria’s sluggish economy.

“We’ve seen area boys [street urchins] switching to become dancers,” said the producer Azzi On The Beat, an early adopter of mara who has stayed true to the sound. “The music is spiritual.”

T he hectic but harmonious sound has become a fixture at raves, which in Nigeria take the form of street-style block-gatherings populated by young people tired of the markup on alcohol at nightclubs and “bottle culture” – the buying of expensive bottles of champagne and spirts in VIP sections, often as a means of flaunting wealth.

Top musicians have been enlisting the sound in search of new hits, but mara’s originators remain relatively unknown, their work often restricted to the thriving underground “TrenchTok” scene.

Khalipha said bookers assumed that mara DJs would have an air of chaos and violence, due to the raw sound of the music and its association with street culture.

Abiola agreed. “[Mara DJs] are not harmful, but they face stereotypes because of their background, how they look and how they dress,” she said. “In my documentary, I wanted people to see these people for who they were … young people innovating and contributing to the cultural identity of this generation. Regardless of where they are from, they deserve to be taken seriously.”

Without institutional backing, the DJs have been learning how to navigate the music industry on the go. When the samples they were using were flagged for copyright issues, they created their own instrumentals from scratch using plugins.

Many artists are self-funded, investing money earned as social media influencers or from royalties into shooting videos and promotion. Female dancers talk of sexual harassment and financial exploitation in the industry.

“The financial challenges are more apparent for the dancers, because people don’t really take dancers seriously,” said Abiola.

Pointing to a square littered with weeds and rubbish, where goats roamed next to a woman sieving black-eyed peas on a tray, Azzi’s 27-year-old manager, Sangokunle Anuoluwapo – known as Kadima – said: “We do most of our videos here.”

D espite the challenges, the people involved in mara harbour dreams of global traction. Support from the French embassy helped Azzi perform at festivals in Uganda and parts of Europe. A few industry friends on the rise or those who Kadima at one point managed also help intermittently with funding or promoting projects for free.

“I understand what we want for this culture so we keep pushing really hard,” said Kadima. “It’s family work, so we try to split revenues among everybody.”

Azzi was given a leg up from the Footprints of David Art Academy, a children’s dance theatre troupe that held performances behind his mother’s shop. He honed his dancing skills, learned how to drum, and met Kadima there. “We were taught how to fight through tough times,” Azzi said.

The art director Seun Awobajo launched the academy in 2005 with the aim of channelling the energy of disadvantaged children into creative endeavours. “[I had] the notion that no child is useless, they are only used less,” he said.

Awobajo is proud of his former wards and the mara scene more generally. “Being proud is an understatement,” he said. “But I think I feel more fulfilled seeing what they’ve become because these are children who the upper class of the society have written off.”

items.title: New Zealand election: final results show ruling coalition needs minor party to govern
items.author: Eva Corlett in Wellington
items.content:
Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election

The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon loses majority and needs support of Opportunity party to remain in power, or country faces another election

The final results of New Zealand’s general election show the incumbent rightwing coalition will need the support of a centrist newcomer party to form a government, and to avoid sending the country back to the polls.

Preliminary results on 7 November handed the National party and its two coalition partners, the populist New Zealand First and libertarian Act parties, a slim two-seat majority, making the election too close to call until final votes were tallied.

On Friday, the electoral commission released the results from nearly 485,000 “special votes” – those cast from overseas or outside a voter’s electorate. National dropped two seats to 40, Labour stayed on 36 seats, the Greens picked up one seat to 17, Act had 13, New Zealand First 12, Opportunity seven and Te Pati Māori five.

The National-led bloc currently has 65 seats. In the 130-seat parliament, 66 seats are needed for a majority.

The National-led coalition has the only realistic path to power – if it can negotiate a deal with Opportunity. If it cannot, New Zealand will likely need to hold another election.

Three electorate seats changed hands following the special votes. Labour won Wairarapa off National with just 81 votes, and took Hamilton East from of National with 173 votes. The Greens won Wellington Bays from Labour with 1,610 votes.

If National applies for a recount and wins back just one of those seats, it could return to power with a slim majority and without needing Opportunity. Applications for a recount must be made by 3 December, and results could take another five days.

Special votes in previous elections have favoured the left, and typically have cost the right one or two seats. Until Friday, a question mark hung over whether National would be able to govern comfortably alongside its coalition partners, or whether it would be forced to cut a deal with the Opportunity party – a newcomer centrist party that incumbent prime minister Christopher Luxon had previously ruled out working with.

After the election, Luxon softened his stance on his initial rule-out, saying he intended to find common ground with the Opportunity party.

On Friday afternoon, Luxon said National will now begin formal negotiations with New Zealand First, Act and Opportunity, but he cautioned discussions would be “challenging” and could take some time.

“Getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly,” Luxon said. “Kiwis won’t thank us for rushing to an agreement that falls apart, or for sending them back to the polls.”

Opportunity, led by Auckland businesswoman Qiulae Wong , has long said it will negotiate first with the party that secures the highest number of seats.

After the final results were announced, Wong confirmed she would speak with Luxon and that her party’s bottom-lines – which include climate and environment policies and capping political donations – were non-negotiable.

The party would focus on bringing New Zealanders a stable government, Wong told media, and she did not rule out heading back to the polls.

“Clearly stability is important. But setting that more hopeful and aspirational vision, where we can come together as much as possible as New Zealanders and move forward, I think is the priority,” she said.

Having Opportunity in parliament was a “pivotal moment” for the country, Wong said.

“I have every expectation that we will get in there and we will deliver, regardless of what shape the government takes.”

Previously, Wong has said its vision for a low-emissions future, and an inclusive New Zealand, will drive its final decision . Its five bottom-line issues include action on New Zealand’s supermarket duopoly, capping political donations, a 10-year cross-party plan for health, ending bottom trawling in the fishing industry and strengthening New Zealand’s climate commitments.

Negotiations with Opportunity could hit a snag with National’s coalition partner New Zealand First. On Friday, Wong confirmed she would not strike a deal if New Zealand First’s leader, the veteran politician Winston Peters, serves as foreign affairs minister – a position he has held on three occasions.

“We think that his behaviour over successive governments is not the kind of behavior that we expect of someone in that position,” she said.

In other points of tension, New Zealand First and Act have diametrically opposed climate policies, and Act are also unlikely to back Opportunity’s drive for political donation reforms.

New Zealand could be facing weeks of negotiations in what could become its first ever four-party coalition. In 2023, negotiations took five weeks. With Christmas just four weeks away, New Zealand may need to wait until 2027 to know the shape of its next government.

items.title: Threat from China looms large over Taiwan’s local elections
items.author: Amy Hawkins and Yu-chen Li in Taipei
items.content:
Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party

Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years, are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Taiwanese officials raise alarm over interference by China in elections that will shape fortunes of ruling party

Taiwanese voters go to the polls on Saturday in closely watched local elections that will shape the fortunes of the ruling Democratic Progressive party (DPP) as it navigates an increasingly precarious set of relationships on the global stage.

Saturday’s vote will choose mayors, council members and other local leaders across 22 districts. Unlike the presidential elections, in which foreign policy is often a key issue, the local elections, held every four years , are largely focused on bread-and-butter issues such as housing affordability and wealth distribution.

Nevertheless, China looms large over the vote, which takes place against the background of intense military pressure from Beijing . China claims Taiwan as part of its territory despite never having ruled the self-governing island. Taiwanese officials have raised the alarm over thousands of incidents of suspected misinformation or election interference, and certain candidates have been subjected to harassment from the Chinese authorities. There have also been reports of hundreds of China-linked AI-generated videos spreading disinformation about Taiwanese politicians disliked by Beijing.

Beijing calls the allegations of election interference “completely fabricated”. Zhu Fenglian, a spokesperson for China’s Taiwan affairs office, said the allegations “stir up anti-China sentiment to win votes”.

Wei-Ting Yen, a political scientist at Academia Sinica, Taiwan’s national research academy, said: “Even though local elections are not about China, the outcome of local elections will have huge implications for cross-strait relations.”

Most races are a tight competition between a candidate from the ruling DPP and the main opposition party, the Kuomintang (KMT). The KMT promotes closer ties with Beijing, and its chair, Cheng Li-wun, travelled to China this year to meet Xi Jinping, China’s leader. Xi has vowed to unify China with Taiwan, and has not ruled out using military action to achieve that aim.

Yen said if the KMT loses some of its traditional strongholds, Beijing “may need to reconsider what is the most effective strategy for influencing Taiwanese people”.

One of the most contentious votes is the race for Taipei mayor, an office that has been held by the KMT for three decades. The DPP has selected as its challenger Puma Shen, a national legislator whom Beijing declared a “diehard separatist” in 2024. It is the first time a candidate under sanctions by Beijing has run to be mayor of Taiwan’s capital city. In the neighbouring New Tapei City race, the DPP’s Su Chiao-hui is also proving to be a ferocious challenger to the incumbent KMT.

Shen said in a recent interview that even if he didn’t win, the capital’s mayoral race was “a slap to China” because it proved that “democracy works here in Taiwan”.

Huang Bo-kai, a 23-year-old law student, said his top concern was cross-strait relations and how US-China relations were evolving. “The world’s three major powers are increasingly willing to flex their muscles: the US attacking Iran, Russia attacking Ukraine. I think Taiwan could very well be the next target [of China],” he told the Guardian.

Taiwan’s president, the DPP’s Lai Ching-te, is detested by Beijing and has taken a bolshier stance on cross-strait relations than his predecessor, Tsai Ing-wen, who was admired for her ability to drum up support in Washington while walking a delicate tightrope to avoid angering China.

Lai has pushed for greater spending on weapons to deter military aggression from China. The government has proposed a record 18% increase in defence spending for next year, including for drones and missiles, taking it above 1tn Taiwan dollars (£23bn) for the first time.

But many Taiwanese voters would rather that money was spent on more immediate economic issues. Lev Nachman, a political scientist at National Taiwan University, said the national leaders of the DPP and KMT had been notably absent from the mayoral races, reflecting the extent to which campaigns were focused on local issues.

Going into the campaigns for the 2028 presidential elections, Lai would “try to take advantage of the momentum that [Shen] and Su have built for the DPP,” Nachman said, noting that support for those candidates would not necessarily translate into support for Lai.

Tony Yeh, a Taipei man in his 70s, said: “To put it simply, the authorities should do more to boost the economy and buy fewer weapons.”

Taiwan’s economy has boomed this year, largely thanks to the pivotal role that its semiconductor industry plays in the global artificial intelligence rally. The economy grew by more than 14% in the first nine months of the year, the fastest rate in 50 years. But nearly 70% of workers earned less than the average monthly wage of 49,152 Taiwan dollars (£1,137) in the same period.

Yeh said: “Most traditional industries are having a really tough time.”

William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “The issues that really are going to determine their votes are livelihood issues including the stagnant wage, the astronomically high housing price, the affordability issue, and how the government can better make sure Taiwan’s incredible economic boom fuelled by the global AI growth is going to be distributed more evenly.”

Other voters have more niche concerns. Walking her dog in a park, Kuo Wei-tong, a nail salon worker, said policies affecting pets were among her top concerns.

“People are having fewer children and getting more cats and dogs,” she said. “I think that’s something worth giving serious consideration to as well.”

items.lbText:
Statement follows death of sisters, aged 15 and 13, in airstrike on residential apartment in Gaza City

Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.

On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip.”

“The number of schoolchildren killed since the beginning of November has now risen to 16,” it added.

The statement follows the death of two sisters, Yusra, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 13, in the early hours of Wednesday in an airstrike targeting a residential apartment in western Gaza City.

Yusra was a pupil at Kafr Qasim school, while her sister Jana attended al-Manar private school.

The ministry added: “The girls’ father, Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Ouf, and their mother, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Ouf, were also killed in the strike which injured several other Palestinians.” The father was a director of internal security services for Hamas in northern Gaza.

Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

On 6 November, Mohammed Nidal Barbakh, 15, was shot by Israeli forces in the Bir 19 area of al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, and later died from his injuries.

He was in the 10th grade at the Muscat school and dreamed of becoming a professional football player.

“That day, after lunch, Mohammed went to the sports academy at 1.30pm to take part in training,” his father, Dr Nidal Mohammed Barbakh, said. “An Israeli tank had advanced and positioned itself on a nearby hill before firing two rounds towards the pitch. One of them ricocheted after hitting a metal object, striking Mohammed in the back and exiting through his neck.

“He was talented and an excellent student. He was killed at the age of 15, on a sports pitch in al-Mawasi, an area where people had been told to go because it was considered safe. I do not absolve the Israeli army of responsibility for what happened. It kills every ambition within us and buries our children’s dreams before they have a chance to come true.”

On 13 November, Israeli artillery shelling killed three people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, including a father and his 12-year-old son, Ahmed Abu Daher, as well as a woman.

Ahmed dreamed of becoming an Arabic language teacher, like his grandfather Saleh, said his mother, Walaa Abu Daher.

“That day, my husband was heading to a condolence gathering in the al-Qastal area, east of Deir al-Balah,” Daher said. “Ahmed asked his father if he could accompany him. While they were at the gathering, they were targeted by Israeli artillery fire. Ahmed ran to ask the people attending the gathering for help. He then rushed back towards his father when a second shell was fired. Shrapnel struck Ahmed in his legs, abdomen and head.

“I cannot describe how deeply their loss has affected me. I feel as though my life stopped that day,” she added.

The Israel Defense Forces have been approached for comment.

Thousands of school-age children and hundreds of education workers have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza, while tens of thousands of children have been unable to attend school regularly.

On Thursday, Israeli attacks killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, including Khaled Abu Nada, the undersecretary of Gaza’s ministry of education, and his wife, according to health officials, as attacks continued despite the ceasefire in the territory.

A few days ago, the ministry of education said Israel’s attacks against students, civilian leaders and teachers were “part of a systematic assault on the Palestinian education system”.

According to Unicef , 98% of school buildings in Gaza have sustained damage, with more than 93% requiring major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, while approximately 81% were directly hit.

Young Palestinians in Gaza face a fourth winter in overcrowded tents and makeshift shelters, with limited access to basic services as the humanitarian and public health crisis deepens.

Children and young people are among those most vulnerable to meningitis, for which Gaza’s health ministry issued an epidemic alert on Tuesday after a sharp rise in infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid.

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza over the last three years, according to the territory’s health ministry. More than 20,000 children have been reported killed by Israeli strikes.

Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum

In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions.

They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets.

Also on display are protective ritual objects, taken by the British from Gaidinliu’s hiding places, which they believed she had used against them. These are a stick with a monkey skull used to ward off evil spirits, and small wooden clubs, traditionally used by Naga people to cast an omen on an enemy.

The exhibition, The Afterlives of Captured Objects , raises questions about the colonial extraction of artefacts from Indigenous communities, which were often originally catalogued using prejudiced and discriminatory language, according to the curator, Clare Harris, a professor of visual anthropology.

For example, Harris said Gaidinliu’s notebooks were derided as “meaningless scribbling” by the colonial anthropologist JP Mills, who collected them. But he also recorded that these writings “gave her immense prestige”, which suggests that they may have been seized as part of British efforts to suppress the religious and political movement that Gaidinliu led, called Heraka.

While most of the objects on display were taken by the British after Gaidinliu abandoned them while on the run, two items were more violently extracted. Textiles displayed on mannequins in the show were taken from a pair of male and female sacred clay figures from a Heraka temple in the village of Kambiron in 1931.

The textiles are shown along with a photograph taken by a British officer of another soldier kneeling with the sacred figures, which were destroyed along with the temple.

“By showing the photograph at the same time, you can make the equation visually about what was extracted by the British there,” said Harris. “The British destroy the temple and they destroy the figures, so they take away the potency of those things.”

The show follows a four-year project by researchers from India and the Universities of Edinburgh and Oxford to digitise the Gaidinliu collection and share it with Naga communities in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Their craftspeople have used the images to revive and revitalise traditional crafts such as basket weaving and textile making, with some of their creations included in the exhibition.

Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at the school of divinity, University of Edinburgh, who co-led the project with Harris, said attempts were also being made to translate Gaidinliu’s notebooks in an effort to reconstruct a new Indigenous language for the Naga people.

He said: “There are some symbols which are recognisable within stories and myths. They may be untranslatable in a conventional sense but they are being used to try and construct a language system.”

The exhibition also aims to raise international recognition of Gaidinliu, who has long been revered as an important leader in the resistance movement that led to Indian independence. After her release from prison in 1947, she became head of a political movement advocating for recognition of a Naga homeland.

Alila Chang, one of Gaidinliu’s grandnieces, said her family felt a deep sense of pride about the exhibition. She said: “These objects are connected to our family’s history and the struggles and sacrifices of our people as well. We want the world to know her struggles and for what reason she fought.”

Chang, who has come to Oxford for the exhibition’s private view, also shared a more personal recollection of Gaidinliu as a “very affectionate grandmother”.

“I remember [her] giving us sweets,” she said, adding how Gaidinliu, who died in 1993, would pray for her and her sibling when they went to school in the morning.

“She will always be in our hearts, but I think she belongs to the world now.”

Six helipads built and feast prepared by 500 cooks for wedding hosted by Anant Singh, an MP charged with murder

It takes a brave soul to try to match the mythic opulence of the wedding arranged by the Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani for his son Anant in 2024. Estimates of the cost for the months-long celebration ran to at least $600m, with world leaders and celebrities among those on the guest list.

Smaller fry though he is, Anant Singh, a legislator in India’s poorest state, Bihar, gave it his best shot on Wednesday, albeit in a rustic rural setting, for the nuptials of his daughter Shivangi Singh, and Rishikesh Kumar, an MBA student from Georgia State University in Atlanta.

About 400,000 guests were hosted across 2.5 hectares at the family home in the village of Nadawa – a staggering figure even by the standards of India’s famed extravagant weddings. Guests were treated to 500,000 pieces of traditional sweets, and a feast prepared by an army of 500 chefs and cooks, Singh’s confidant Munna Singh told Agence France-Presse. One thousand kgs of mutton were reportedly used for kebabs and curries. Six makeshift helipads were erected for VIPs flying in from across India.

Kumar arrived at the venue in sunglasses and waving an orange scarf in a convoy of 151 cars (Hindus consider uneven numbers to be lucky). Among the gifts for the groom was a Land Rover Defender.

The roads leading to the venue were so choked with cars before the wedding that one guest escaped the gridlock, The Times of India reported, by jumping on a tractor and driving across the surrounding fields.

Guests were also treated to elaborate flower arrangements featuring blooms imported from China, and a fireworks display.

Instead of a DJ for entertainment, Singh planned a horse race. Gatecrashers clambered up into trees and on to electricity towers to catch a glimpse of the race, but the chaos and tumult was so great it had to be cancelled at the 11th hour. Lying around somewhere amid the wedding detritus was the SUV that would have gone to the winner.

Singh is a controversial figure. Elected five times to the state assembly, he has 28 criminal cases pending against him ranging from murder and attempted murder to extortion and kidnapping. All the cases are listed on the website of the Association for Democratic Reforms, an NGO trying to improve governance and strengthen democracy. Singh denies any wrongdoing.

In a television interview before the wedding, he pooh poohed the idea that there was anything unusual about the scale of the wedding preparations. “I laid on exactly the same thing for my elder daughter,” he said.

India’s wedding season has just kicked off. Between now and 15 December, an estimated 5.2m weddings are expected to take place across the country.
