items.lbText:
The US and Russia’s candidate for secretary general is on a charm offensive. Can she overcome London’s resistance to her bid?

L ana Nusseibeh is in Britain this week, attempting to present herself as a potential future UN secretary general, and shift the focus from her past as a United Arab Emirates diplomat who denied the country’s role in arming a militia accused of war crimes and genocide in Sudan’s four-year civil war.

It is a high-risk strategy that involves meeting ministers, MPs, academics and holding a public event with the UN Association.

Labelled by many British NGOs and others as an apologist for war crimes, Nusseibeh is presenting herself as a skilled diplomat with the network to put the UN back at the centre of mediation, development and human rights.

“These are very geopolitical times,” she said in an interview. “You need a geopolitical secretary general, because the fact is these geopolitical ruptures are not going away. These fissures in the international system are not going to dissolve any time soon.”

Nusseibeh had a setback last Friday, when three permanent members of the UN security council, China, France and the UK , all voted to “discourage” her candidature. The UN’s electoral system requires that she secure nine positive votes from the 15-strong security council, and no discouragement from the permanent five (P5) before being recommended to the UN general assembly.

She has the backing of the US and Russia, and thinks her cause is not lost. “Sometimes, the use of the veto is tactical. Sometimes, it’s a holding position, sometimes it’s a leveraging position. There are a number of different theories”.

The centre of the resistance to Nusseibeh’s candidacy is probably London, and specifically the Foreign Office, the penholder on Sudan at the UN, and this may explain the UK political blitz.

When questioned about her role in Sudan, she asked that her candidacy be seen in the round, highlighting her role in forcing humanitarian aid into Gaza, her support for Afghan women and promoting interfaith tolerance.

“Like every candidate, I come from somewhere, but the independence of the incoming secretary general is the key to their credibility.

“I’ve taken a leave of absence from my role in [the] UAE government in order to independently campaign for this role. But I think that if I was secretary general, Sudan would be the litmus test of success for any incoming secretary because it’s such a horrific humanitarian crisis.”

The war in Sudan, which erupted in April 2023 after a power struggle between the ​military and the Rapid Support Forces, has displaced more than 14 million people and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. Multiple regional powers, including the UAE , have backed different local proxies since the beginning of the conflict in an attempt to win influence and strategic resources.

The UAE has long been accused of supporting the RSF in Sudan, a charge repeatedly denied by Nusseibeh, who has publicly disputed the findings of UN investigators.

A UN panel of experts suggested last month that the UAE had supplied crucial support to the RSF.

Asked if she regretted dissembling during her time as a diplomat, by denying the UAE had armed the RSF, or her personal role in challenging the UN reports critical of the UAE, Nusseibeh said she regretted that “the Sudanese civil war had continued for so long”.

Nusseibeh added: “But I don’t think saying that is enough for the Sudanese people and the people in the surrounding countries where they’ve also felt the impact of this war, or for the victims of sexual violence and in this conflict, the atrocities committed in El Fasher without accountability, and the use of chemical weapons against the civilian population; all of these are a litany of suffering that has been inflicted on the Sudanese people.”

Asked if the UAE had been supplying weapons to the RSF in a breach of a UN embargo, she replied: “I’m aware of the allegations. I haven’t read the last UN panel of experts report, but I’m not going to comment as I’m no longer a UAE official. In this campaign, I am a secretary general candidate.

“As secretary general, I would fully back the findings of all UN panel of experts reports and I’m aware that I think several countries have been mentioned in various reports.”She later added: “I would call out countries that are supplying arms to any of the parties, including those in the RSF … this needs a process that requires accountability for atrocities that have been committed. That it needs to be a process primarily led by the Sudanese people.”

Nusseibeh said she was willing to take risks to mediate and to put UN values, expertise and its development toolkit at the centre of disputes. Her analysis of contemporary diplomacy was that the world had descended into a default setting of non-cooperation, and the UN needed to restate the case for collaboration between nations as being in the self-interest of everyone.

The UN had been missing from too many conflicts, she argued, and she would set up a mediation board to try to use the full UN toolkit, ranging from confidence-building measures to development to secure peace. “What’s missing is this idea of a secretary general that is a strategist and a mediator-in-chief that is looking at the sort of the blips on the dashboard of conflict and saying, ‘How do we deploy to have maximum impact for most effective use of resource and cost?’ Because resources are not going up, they’re going down. I mean, we’re looking at, since 2010, 40% increase in military spending. So we’re using a lot of hard power as countries and systems to deter, but it’s not actually working.”

That would require some prioritisation at the UN – it has 4,000 different open mandates.

Her intelligence and skills as a diplomat are not in question. However, her track record over Sudan is.…

items.title: China reserves right to take ‘necessary measures’ after Trump’s new tariff proposals
items.author: Rebecca Bailey and agencies
items.content:
Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’, while Brazil ‘will not yield to this type of threat’

Beijing has said it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” after Donald Trump’s administration proposed new tariffs on goods from China and other major trading partners, triggering a global backlash.

Among the suggested levies on 14 major trading partners announced on Wednesday, China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. It would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Brazil indignant about proposed tariffs on sugar and aircraft, while Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’

Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU

Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday: “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.

It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

Brazil was singled out in the announcement after trade talks stalled. The Trump administration claimed on Wednesday that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries.

The new tariffs are being imposed under a law which allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”

The Trump administration’s new tariff rates would be capped at lower ​levels ‌agreed under ​trade deals ​that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.

The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. The US said China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%. The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027.

A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer said. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”

Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”

The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the US to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said.

Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.

It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties.”

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.

Taiwan was also singled out for new tariffs, but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech product which account for ​over 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.

Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, and Thailand.

Tokyo’s top government spokesman, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

And Singapore’s government said it was “very disappointed” with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidising manufacturing.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

However Democratic Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”…

items.lbText:
Public Committee Against Torture in Israel examined 42 complaints against Shin Bet interrogators over past decade

Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from Palestinian prisoners, sometimes documenting abuse in official records or granting advanced approval for “special measures” in interrogation, according to a report from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI).

This dangerous practice risked leading to irreversible miscarriages of justice, as Israel moved to implement a racist new death penalty law that targets Palestinians, the report said.

PCATI examined 42 cases in which Palestinians filed complaints about the use of torture by Shin Bet interrogators over the last decade.

More than three-quarters said they confessed after the use of “torture or other illegal methods”, and one in 10 provided incriminating statements about other people under torture.

“When it comes to Palestinian detainees, the Israeli legal system officially sanctions torture as a tool for extracting confessions, regardless of whether the content of those confessions is true,” said Sari Bashi, the executive director of PCATI.

“Torture as a tool of interrogation is particularly egregious given initiatives to impose the death penalty in Israel for the first time since 1962.”

Over the years, in hundreds of testimonies , Palestinian detainees have consistently described interrogations employing extreme sleep deprivation, physical violence such as slapping and kicking, threats, sexual violence and being held in stress positions.

Some of this abuse is also laid out in the official records of Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security service. PCATI details the case of a Palestinian lawyer arrested in February 2019 who was subjected to extreme sleep deprivation.

During an interrogation period lasting 27.5 days, or 660 hours, he was questioned for more than 552 hours, an average of 20 hours a day, with one session lasting nearly 48 hours. Some of the remaining 108 hours were spent travelling to and attending detention hearings.

In a 1999 ruling, Israel’s supreme court explicitly prohibited sleep deprivation as a deliberate interrogation method. Despite this, the lawyer was convicted of involvement in shooting attacks based on information extracted during this period.

The state inspector for complaints about Shin Bet interrogations (Mavtan) ruled that the interrogations took place in accordance with procedures, PCATI said.

More than 1,680 torture complaints were filed between 2001 and 2024 with Mavtan. None have led to an indictment.

Other cases are indirectly documented in Israeli judicial records, although judges rarely accept testimony about torture of Palestinians, PCATI said.

In one case, a detainee’s false confession, made under torture, was used as evidence by prosecutors. The man was released after his lawyer presented proof that he was not present at the scene of the crime, PCATI said.

Sleep deprivation was the most frequently used form of torture in complaints examined by PCATI, but more than half included the use of stress positions and other forms of physical violence.

Israel is a signatory to the UN convention against torture, but its legal system has effectively codified the use of violence and abuse where it is deemed “necessary” to extract life-saving information, PCATI said.

In a “necessity interrogation” or “military interrogation”, Shin Bet officials torture detainees “after consulting with their superiors and following an internal procedure for documenting their decisions and conduct”, the report said.

“[A] supposedly narrow exception ballooned and developed into a sprawling system of legal and administrative exceptions that swallowed the so-called rule, enabling the use of violence while maintaining the appearance of prohibition,” it continued.

There is no publicly available information on the scale of “necessity interrogations” inside the Shin Bet, PCATI said. They are an urgent concern as Israel moves to end a de facto moratorium on the death penalty, which had stood since the 1962 execution of the Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann.

“The death penalty is always wrong, because it’s cruel, irreversible and negates the right to life. No one should be executed, particularly not in a system tainted by systematic violence,” Bashi said.

In March, the Knesset passed a racist law allowing the execution of Palestinians convicted of terror charges over deadly attacks, but not Jewish Israelis who commit similar crimes.

In the occupied West Bank , where Palestinians are tried in military courts, execution is now the default punishment for a defendant found guilty of deadly terror attacks.

The legislation drew fierce international criticism, including from the UN’s high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, who warned that it would constitute a war crime if enacted.

A separate law empowers a special tribunal to impose death sentences in cases arising from the 7 October 2023 attacks.

Even in rare cases where courts have excluded confessions obtained under torture, Israeli case law allows prosecutors to use information derived from them as evidence to secure convictions.

PCATI said that as detention conditions worsened after October 2023, rights groups documented a sharp rise in violence by Israeli prison guards and soldiers , including beatings, attacks with dogs, electric shocks, threats and rape.

At least 103 Palestinian detainees have died in Israeli custody since 7 October 2023. Of 10 postmortems reviewed by Physicians for Human Rights Israel , five showed signs of physical assault and six showed evidence of medical neglect.

The Israel Prison Service said “all prisoners are held in accordance with the law”. The Shin Bet and Israel’s justice ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

items.lbText:
Yuki Imai being held in Moscow on allegations he conducted ‘espionage’ while working for a newspaper in Sakhalin island in Russia’s far east

The wife of a Japanese journalist who has been detained in Russia for more than a month on suspicion of spying has issued an emotive appeal for his release.

Yuki Imai, a reporter for the Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested in mid-October as he was preparing to return to Japan from a two-year assignment at the Japanese newspaper’s bureau in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, on the island of Sakhalin in Russia’s far east.

Russian authorities alleged that Imai had been “conducting espionage activities” on the island, collecting information about Russian defence capabilities he intended to pass on to Japanese intelligence. Both the newspaper and Japan’s prime minster, Sanae Takaichi , have denied the claims.

His detention has inflamed tensions between Tokyo and Moscow and prompted Takaichi to request Imai’s release during a meeting with the Russian leader Vladimir Putin at last week’s Apec summit in China.

The arrest comes amid rapidly deteriorating ties between Japan and Russia, triggered by Tokyo’s support for Ukraine and a longstanding dispute over islands in the Kuril chain near Sakhalin that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories. Japan claims the four islands closest to its territory – the nearest is less than 4km from Hokkaido – which Russia has administered since the dying days of the second world war.

In a statement released to media organisations through the Hokkaido Shimbun, Imai’s wife, Nozomi Imai, said her husband’s plight meant his family were “trapped in grief”.

“Since his detention, his parents and I have spent every day worrying about him” she said in the statement, published in Japanese, English and Russian. Recalling the moment she saw TV footage of her husband being taken away by Russian authorities, she said: “I could hardly breathe. It felt as if my heart were being ripped apart.”

She added: “No one could remain calm after seeing a beloved family member with his arms bound behind his back. In the video, I could even see the souvenirs in his suitcase – the gifts he was bringing home for us. I could not sleep even for a moment that night. When morning came, it still did not feel real. I could not even cry.”

Imai, 34, has barely seen his infant daughter, who was born during his posting to Russia. “He had been so looking forward to coming home,” Nozomi Imai wrote. “During his posting, our daughter was born. She is now 21 months old, and he loves her more than words can say. He had even said excitedly that he wanted to be the one to pick her up from daycare on the very day he got home.”

Japanese diplomats have been permitted to visit Imai only twice since he was detained, although he has had several meetings with lawyers appointed by his employer.

Japan’s ambassador to Moscow, Akira Muto, said he had met the journalist at Lefortovo detention centre in Moscow this week and that he appeared to be in good health. Japanese embassy officials were also granted access to Imai at the end of October.

The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai had been engaged in “ordinary news gathering” on Sakhalin, adding the newspaper did “not conduct reporting or gather information based on government directions”.

Shortly after his arrest, Takaichi denied Imai had been spying. “There is no such fact,” she told reporters, adding that “the protection of Japanese nationals is extremely important right now, and we intend to focus our efforts on that.”

Concerns are growing that Moscow will seek to make an example of Imai in protest at Japan’s support for sanctions imposed after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Russia’s Federal Security Service, which is investigating Imai, has not commented publicly since it announced the reporter’s arrest. His detention is scheduled to expire on 12 December but could be extended, the Kyodo news agency said.

The Hokkaido Shimbun said Imai, whose grandfather was born on Sakhalin, was an admirer of Russian culture who had used his position to promote grassroots exchanges.He even hosted Russian visitors at his home in the Hokkaido city of Nemuro.

Nozomi Imai, who said she and her husband had met as students through their shared love of Russian films and novels, said his detention was taking a toll on his ageing parents.

“They worry whether they will ever see their beloved only son again in their lifetime,” she wrote. “Yuki Imai is not only a journalist. He is a beloved son, husband, and father. Please – please return this precious papa to his little daughter.”

Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 21 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charred

A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the health ministry.

The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, the ministry said.

At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.

The Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.

The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.

Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.

In January, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

items.lbText:
Judgment casts doubt on evidence linking aid workers to Hamas and says humanitarian efforts in Gaza were damaged

A UN tribunal has cast doubt on the evidence used to justify the sacking of Palestinian UN aid workers in 2024, saying it was based “almost entirely” on unproven assertions from the Israeli government and had damaged humanitarian operations in Gaza.

The judgment, seen by the Guardian, raises fresh questions about the decision by the UN Relief and Works Agency (Unrwa), the main humanitarian organisation working in Gaza, to sack members of staff. It was taken on the basis of Israeli allegations of involvement in the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023.

The nine workers had their contracts terminated in January 2024 “in the interests of the agency” and were told in termination letters that the allegations against them were “very serious and credible”. The dismissals were confirmed after a UN investigation found they might have been involved in the 7 October attacks.

The decision, which was taken by former Unrwa commissioner general Philippe Lazzarini after consultation with the UN secretary general, António Guterres, was apparently made in the hope that appeasing Israel and its allies would allow humanitarian work to continue in Gaza .

Critics warned at the time that the decision, on the basis of allegations rather than evidence, compromised the UN’s integrity and had the opposite effect, giving credence to unproven allegations.

The dismissals failed to prevent the Biden administration ordering a pause in funding, a measure that was echoed temporarily by other backers, leading to a financial shortfall of $450m (£340m).

“I have always said on the record that the Israeli allegations against Unrwa were the mother of all lies,” said Chris Gunness, a former Unrwa spokesperson. “Sacking the workers without any evidence confirmed their guilt unfairly, in the minds of journalists, led 16 top donors to abandon Unrwa and produced the worst financial crisis in the agency’s history, from which it may never recover.”

The Unrwa dispute tribunal that ruled in favour of one of its sacked workers, Abu Awad, described the Israeli allegations as unsupported and of “limited evidentiary value and reliability”.

The tribunal also found that an internal UN investigation had not interviewed the 19 staff members initially accused by Israel of involvement in the 7 October attacks because of “safety and security” concerns.

“The allegations against the applicant and the other staff members, it seems, are therefore based almost entirely on information in Israel’s possession,” the tribunal said.

It cast doubt on intercepted mobile phone conversations and messages offered by Israel as evidence, noting that one case had involved mistaken identity based on a cloned sim card, a common phenomenon in Gaza.

It also said that voice recognition claims made by Israel were dubious and some transcripts of conversations were found by UN investigators not to support claims that they proved links to Hamas or the 7 October attacks.

The allegation against Awad was that he was a “platoon commander” in Hamas’s military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades, a claim he rejected. He was not alleged to have physically taken part in the 7 October attack and witness statements to the tribunal said he was on an Unrwa staff bus as normal.

The specific allegation against Awad was that he “had been instructed in a telephone call intercepted by Israeli intelligence to monitor the events of 7 October 2023, while simultaneously receiving Hamas intelligence updates related to the attacks”.

The tribunal said the Israeli security services had failed to clarify who was alleged to have made the call to Awad and in what way the mobile phone that received the call was associated with him.

Unrwa did not respond to a request for comment. Asked by the tribunal to provide evidence underpinning the dismissal of the workers, the agency cited the Israeli government as well as a report in the Times of Israel and another on the website UN Watch, a pro-Israel pressure group that has campaigned against Unrwa.

In its ruling, the tribunal said Unrwa’s claim that the cited sources had informed the decision to dismiss the workers was “open to some doubt” because all the supporting documents it had submitted were produced after the disputed decision was made on 26 January 2024.

Lazzarini, a Swiss humanitarian expert who left the commissioner general post in March, said he understood the tribunal’s finding might be appealed so he could not discuss the case in detail. In February 2024, he admitted his decision to sack the workers represented “reverse due process” in that the investigation followed the dismissal.

“My judgment, based on this going public, true or untrue, was I need to take the swiftest and boldest decision to show that as an agency we take this allegation seriously,” he said, adding that “the ability of the entire agency to continue to operate and deliver critical humanitarian assistance was at stake”.

The tribunal said it could not decide on the allegations against Awad but ruled that Unrwa had failed to produce evidence supporting its decision to sack him. It awarded him a year’s pay and $5,000 for “moral damages”.

In the wake of its allegations against the sacked workers, Israel claimed that Unrwa was heavily infiltrated by Hamas and its parliament voted in 2024 to ban the agency from operating in Israel or in the occupied Palestinian territories.

The international court of justice stated in October 2025 , however, that “Israel has not substantiated its allegations that a significant part of Unrwa’s employees are members of Hamas … or other terrorist factions”.

items.lbText:
Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held

Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one hostage-taker was killed.

Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.

When masked and armed assailants stormed the supermarket at about 8.30am on Tuesday local time, 30 people including customers and employees were taken hostage, many of whom could be seen through windows with their hands and feet tied. Ten had already been released over the course of the day.

When, after 17 hours in captivity, the final 20 people were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday, four of the hostage-takers were arrested and one was killed.

In a video posted outside the supermarket – about 6 miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls, which are visited by thousands of tourists every year – De la Espriella celebrated the end of the operation.

“One of the criminals was killed. They were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages; they rejected that opportunity and we acted forcefully,” he said. He appeared with a gun on his waist, as he has on several other occasions in public as part of his populist security rhetoric.

The president arrived in Cartagena late on Tuesday afternoon from Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he had been dealing with the aftermath of another attack on Monday night, when a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.

More than 20 people were injured and a security guard was killed, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).

De la Espriella, however, denied that the supermarket hostage-taking had been carried out by a “terrorist group”, as he describes the groups involved in Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict, saying instead that those responsible were common criminals.

The president said they had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle but, after being spotted by private security – who then alerted police – they took refuge in the supermarket.

Commenting on what he called an “extraordinary” rescue operation, De la Espriella said his government was acting out of “the need to defend our people and go after all the criminals with an iron fist”.

The daylong hostage siege took place on a symbolic day for security in Colombia: the 10th anniversary of the country’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas.

In office for just over three months, the president – previously a lawyer and businessman – is a fierce critic of the peace deal and has focused his government on returning to a strategy of full-on confrontation with criminal groups, breaking completely with the “total peace” plan of his predecessor, the leftist Gustavo Petro.

Although some indicators show slight improvements in areas such as homicides and kidnappings, recent days have been marked by a strong response from criminal groups: in addition to the car bombing, another guerrilla group carried out the first-ever drone attack on a departmental capital on Monday.

On Tuesday night, five departments were left without electricity, and De la Espriella said criminals used explosives to bring down power pylons.

“These criminal acts constitute the response of terrorist groups to the forceful offensive being carried out by the national government to restore order and security across the country,” he said.

items.lbText:
Chip Wilson said men importing brides from Thailand was due to women waiting too long to have children

The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand , in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference.

Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it aims to create space for “candid conversations about the barriers women face both in business and society”.

Wilson’s talk on 23 November, titled “Little Black Stretchy Pants” after his memoir, was billed as an “intimate, fireside chat” offering insight into the “mind and instincts of the man himself”. It was moderated by Nuvyn Peters, CEO of Axis Connects.

There is no publicly available video of the event, but the Guardian spoke with people who attended it and reviewed social media posts from those present. Outrage over the event was first reported by the Globe and Mail.

According to people who were there, Wilson told the audience that companies would be reluctant to hire a 22-year-old woman because she might become pregnant at 23 and take maternity leave. He went on to suggest that women were waiting too long to have children, prompting men to import brides from Thailand.

“There were audible gasps in the room and everyone was clearly uncomfortable. It was a mix of disengaging, walking out and also just complete shock of what was being said on stage,” one person said.

“I am floored that Axis gave this man a platform. We all were saying before the event it was surprising he was there – and it’s clear that [Wilson] runs in the organizer’s circles after she opened with the fact that they go on walks [at a Vancouver mountain] together.”

The event, which was supposed to run for an hour, was cut short at 45 minutes.

The remarks are not the first time Wilson has attracted criticism for his comments about women and their bodies. He stepped down as chair of Lululemon’s board in 2013 after the company’s signature black yoga pants were criticized for being see-through and Wilson blamed the problem on the body types of some customers.

On Monday, he reportedly told the group that those prior comments about body types had been “misconstrued” and said he was referring to women who wear sizes that are too small.

Wilson, who is believed to be worth more than C$6bn , has not had a leadership role at Lululemon for several years but remains a major shareholder.

He also reportedly told the audience that poverty had largely been eradicated, and that he was looking forward to going to space with Elon Musk.

Audience members also said Wilson suggested that men were better suited to helm clothing companies that catered to women, because they knew what looked good on women’s bodies. He said the same was true of women who lead companies focused on men’s fashion.

“We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the Leadership Forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects,” Peters said in a statement. “We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community. His comments also underscore an uncomfortable reality: attitudes and assumptions that hold women back in the workplace and in leadership have not disappeared. Challenging those attitudes is central to the work and ethos of Axis Connects.”

Wilson’s spokesperson pointed to the work the Lululemon founder has done to mentor and “empower” women in leadership roles over the years and said his efforts “speak for themselves”. A number of women who were early employees of the company and worked closely with Wilson became millionaires when the company went public, he has previously noted in his memoir, and have gone on to found their own businesses.

More than 700 women attended the conference, many representing organizations they worked for. One person said the experience left her “irate”, adding that it was also indicative of what women continued to tolerate.

“It’s just sad that this is what women still have to deal with, in a forum literally for women.”

items.lbText:
Muhammad Zeeshan Ali – the first Pakistani to reach orbit – greeted with Chinese ‘space handshake’ at Tiangong station

China has flown the first foreign astronaut to its Tiangong space station, starting what it says will be the globalisation of its space operations as the US-led International Space Station (ISS) enters its final years of operation.

Floating through a hatch to enter Tiangong, Pakistan’s Muhammad Zeeshan Ali grinned broadly as he was embraced by the onboard crew in what China’s space agency called the country’s first foreign “space handshake”.

Tiangong, completed in 2022, is the jewel in the crown of China’s space programme. The government has invested billions into its celestial ambitions in recent years to catch up with the US and Russia, two of the five partners involved in the ISS, along with Europe, Japan and Canada. After 25 years of continuous occupation, the ISS is set to cease operations from 2030, according to Nasa.

On Wednesday China’s president, Xi Jinping, told his Pakistani counterpart Beijing was “willing to work with all countries … to uphold the banner of the peaceful use of outer space”.

Ali was part of the crew of Shenzhou 24, the most recent iteration of the series of missions that rotate astronauts in the space station every six months. He is the first Pakistani to reach orbit.

“Sending another country’s astronaut to space is a major undertaking,” Blaine Curcio, the managing director at Orbital Gateway Consulting, told the Guardian. “Pakistan is putting a lot of trust into Beijing by having him fly into space on a Chinese-built rocket. There are also considerations related to security: Ali is getting detailed insights into China’s crewed space programme … It makes China better prepared to do it again, and also makes it clear to other countries that China is open to this type of collaboration.”

Space cooperation between China and Pakistan dates back to the early 1990s. China has launched Pakistani satellites and a Pakistani-built rover ‌is also due to fly on a Chinese lunar mission around 2028.

Shenzhou 24 blasted off from the Jiuquan launch centre in north-west China against a pink-tinged dawn sky on Wednesday, footage showed, and first docked with the space station three and a half hours later.

Ali, a 40-year-old Pakistan air force pilot and payload specialist, will conduct experiments including one cultivating microalgae as a potential food and another testing the effects of spaceflight on quinoa seeds. To prepare for the mission, he ​trained for seven months in Beijing, including intensive Chinese-language classes.

At a press conference the day before the launch, Ali recited a line from a classical Chinese poem. Commander Tang Hongbo told reporters that differences in language and culture had made learning to work together more challenging, but that the effort had paid off.

Ali will not stay for the six-month term usually demanded of Tiangong astronauts. Instead, he will return to earth with two of the Shenzhou 23 crew while its commander, Zhu Yangzhu, will remain to complete another milestone – the first full-year stay in space by a Chinese astronout.

Beijing’s accelerated achievements in the skies have spooked its rivals. China is the third country to put humans in orbit and has landed robotic rovers on Mars and the moon, where it hopes to send crewed missions within the next decade. In racing to the moon before 2030, Beijing is competing with the US’s Artemis programme . The US has excluded China from the ISS since 2011, banning Nasa from collaborating with Beijing. In 2025 Nasa went further by blocking Chinese citizens from its facilities altogether.

“We know that China is quite keen to develop Tiangong as an international hub,” said Curcio, pointing to China Manned Space Agency documents published in coordination with the UN outlining “resources for international cooperation” onboard the station.

In the future, he said, he would expect countries such as Brazil and Egypt to seek out the opportunity to send astronauts on Chinese missions. He added: “I think when the ISS is retired, if there is no western replacement (government or commercial), then yes, we may eventually see European or other ISS-involved countries – like Russia – send astronauts to Tiangong.”

items.lbText:
Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park

A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon .

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.

“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media .

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.

Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund .

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation , which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.

A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”
